extracted.intended_audience: young authors and literary writers preparing to publish (periodicals, essays, books)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic guidance for authors about language choice, coinage of terms, philosophic clarity, and the business/practicalities of publishing (subscriptions, trade publishing, pricing, logistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantry — suitability of words to time/place/company
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry consists in the use of words unsuitable to the time, place, and company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the man of the world who insists on only common conversational terms in scientific disquisition and the man of letters who misestimates his audience are pedants. The language chosen should suit the audience and context; scholarly ostentation is more tolerable than contemptuous ignorance. Example contrasts: the 'language of the market' would be pedantic in schools, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer new technical terms to reusing old words with new meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: When teaching abstract or scientific subjects, either use old words with new meanings or introduce new terms; the latter mode is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using old words with new meanings (example: Darwin in Zoonomia) requires readers to both learn a new definition and unlearn an old habitual meaning, a twofold exertion. Thus coin or adopt precise new terminology (as Linnaeus did) to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore obsolete appropriate terms rather than coin anew
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is possible to recall an appropriate term that had become obsolete, it is a less evil to restore it than to coin a new word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an older term fits the needed sense, restoring it aids comprehension and memory; coinage should be a secondary choice when no suitable historic term exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin new terms only to convey genuinely new senses
rubrics_metrics.description: If one must convey a new sense, a new term can both aid recollection and prevent confusion with existing meanings (example: 'esemplastic' coined from Greek to mean 'to shape into one').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coinage is defensible when it prevents confusion with the usual import of an existing word, but beware of 'pedantry' — the new term must be suitable to time/place/company and genuinely necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose precise philosophical terminology (revive venerable terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt or re-introduce precise terms (examples: 'sensuous' for passive perception; 'objective' and 'subjective'; discriminate 'reason' and 'understanding') to make essential distinctions in metaphysical and speculative writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historically authoritative vocabulary when it clarifies distinctions indispensable to sound speculation. Authority from earlier divines and philosophers can justify reviving terms. Examples given: use 'sensuous' not 'sensual'; 'intuition' for immediateness of knowledge; reintroduce 'objective'/'subjective' for percipere/percipi.

rubrics_metrics.name: First lesson of philosophic discipline — attend to kinds, not degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Wean attention from degrees of things (vocabulary of common life) to the kind abstracted from degree; focus on essential kinds in philosophical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophic writing should direct readers to conceptual kinds rather than merely comparative degrees; e.g., teach chemical students not to be startled by disquisitions on latent heat. This supports introduction of precise terminology and conceptual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor language register to audience and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using language inappropriate to the intended audience (the market vs. the schools); match register (colloquial, technical, learned) to circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same expression may be pedantic or fitting depending on company; assess whether scholarly terms will be intelligible and welcome to your readers. The 'mere man of the world' demanding only conversational terms is as pedantic as the scholar who misreads his audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware trusting subscription lists and subscriber counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place blind trust in the number of names on a subscription list: names may be inauthentic, extorted, volunteered without intent to pay, or surrendered in haste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: many subscribers dropped soon after initial numbers; an Earl who retained many issues but reproved the author for sending them. Verify authority of subscribers and expect attrition; financial planning should assume nonpayment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attempting to unite the roles of author and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to perform both author and publisher functions is imprudent; better to sell copyright or work with the trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-publishing requires extra capital, risk, and labor (buying paper, paying printers, storing stock) often costing more than trade publication. The pragmatic advice: sell the copyright for at least one edition for the highest offer to gain peace of mind (e.g., 'fifty pounds and ease of mind' preferable to uncertain large sums coupled with anxiety).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the economics and logistics of publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing entails costs and delays: buying paper in advance, stamp/post taxes, carriage, printing, and irregular conveyance; these affect cash flow and risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: having to lay in stamped paper eight weeks beforehand, pay for sheets before receiving subscription money, and inability to collect money for early numbers without paying postages. Anticipate such costs and the impact of postal slowness and distribution delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use publishing grievances as pretext for calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not morally denigrate booksellers or trade individuals for systemic or customary trade practices they inherit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booksellers take laws and customs as they find them; personal invective against individuals for practices of the trade is unwise, unmanly, immoral, and calumnious. Critique systemic issues prudently and avoid attacking individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage controversial content in periodicals to avoid losing readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing strong controversial essays (e.g., on religion or politics) can rapidly alienate large portions of subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an essay against fast days cost near five hundred subscribers; subsequent political stances lost more. When running a periodical, balance conviction with awareness of subscribers' expectations; unexpected positions may lead to mass cancellations and financial ruin.
